Île de Ré 2026 · one night en route

Where we stop on Friday 4 September

Four hotels that pass one hard test: a photograph that actually shows people dining outdoors. Ranked on the outdoor room first, because that was the point.

The shortlist at a glance

Drive times are estimates from Calais via the A16 and A28, for comparing options rather than planning to the minute. “Indicative night” is one double room, two dogs and dinner for two.

Where they are

All four sit in the corridor the A28 already takes us down — none is a real detour.

The numbers are the ranking. Gold is Port des Roches, the only one with dining on grass.

Port des Roches and Hôtel de France are both in the Loir valley, twenty minutes apart — so they are natural alternates if one is full.

Positions are plotted from coordinates and are approximate; the dashed line is the Calais → Rouen → Le Mans → Tours → Ré corridor, not a routed path.

The four, in order

Every photograph below was checked by eye before it earned its place here.

1

Auberge du Port des Roches

Luché-Pringé, Sarthe — Loir valley

The only one with tables actually on the grass

The outdoor dining

Tables and chairs set on the grass on the bank of the Loir, under mature trees, plus a parasol terrace in front of the inn. The tourist board describes “a terrace and garden at the water’s edge… much appreciated for summer lunches and dinners”, and the photographs bear it out — this is the one that matches what you actually asked for.

Worth knowing

Its own domain (aubergeduportdesroches.fr) no longer resolves — book by phone via the Michelin or tourist-board listing. Last dinner seating 21:00, so arrive in good time.

2

La Mère Hamard

Semblançay, Indre-et-Loire

Prettiest terrace of the four, and dinner every single night

The outdoor dining

A walled courtyard terrace under a wisteria canopy, festoon lights overhead, tables properly laid with white linen. Not grass — a village-inn courtyard — but by some distance the most attractive outdoor room of the four.

Worth knowing

Its garden is a separate space for lounging — dinner is served on the courtyard terrace, not on the lawn.

3

Hôtel de France

La Chartre-sur-le-Loir, Sarthe

The only one that puts dogs-in-the-restaurant in writing

The outdoor dining

A brick-paved garden terrace with tables under big parasols, screened by greenery, and a separate lawned garden running down to the Loir. Honest village-hotel furniture — green plastic chairs, not linen — so it is a step down in polish from the other two.

Worth knowing

The only one of the four whose kitchen is not in the Michelin restaurant selection, and its room and menu prices are not published anywhere — so it is the one real unknown on cost. Its case now rests entirely on the dogs-in-the-restaurant wording, since the triple rooms that were the other argument for it are no longer needed.

4

Auberge du Bon Laboureur

Chenonceaux, Indre-et-Loire

The best kitchen and the only no-size-limit dog policy — but the longest day

The outdoor dining

Dinner is on a shaded terrace whose own wording is “a peaceful view over the gardens” — you look at the garden rather than sit in it. That said, its gallery does show a bistro table and chairs standing out on the lawn, so a table on the grass is plainly something they could set.

Worth knowing

An hour longer than the target first day, and comfortably the most expensive. Upside: two minutes from Château de Chenonceau for the Saturday morning.

Two of us, so one large double is all we need. That removes the second-room problem entirely and brings every figure above down — Port des Roches to around €205–250 for the night, dinner included. Worth noting the Île de Ré villa is still booked for three adults, which is a separate question.

The open question is the one that has been there all along: whether the dogs may sit with us at the table outside. Only Hôtel de France puts that in writing. It is one phone call per hotel, alongside asking whether they will set a table on the grass — and, at Hôtel de France and Port des Roches, what a room actually costs.

Dropped, and why

Three of the original five failed the photograph test; three more were considered as replacements and rejected on the criteria.

  • Les Hautes Roches — RochecorbonWebsite returns 404 on every path — root, /le-restaurant, /galerie. No photographs obtainable. Still in the 2026 Michelin guide and still trading under new management, so it is reachable by phone, but it cannot be shown.
  • L’Aubinière — Saint-Ouen-les-VignesNo outdoor dining photo exists on the site. Its “terrasse” shot is sun loungers on the pool deck, the garden shot is an empty lawn, and every restaurant image is indoors or a plated dish.
  • Château de Noirieux — BriollayGallery is almost entirely interiors and veranda dining rooms. The only outdoor frame is a close-up of a salad on a table — it never shows the terrace.
  • Domaine de la Tortinière — MontbazonConsidered as a replacement and rejected: dogs are €25/night in rooms but explicitly not allowed in the restaurant.
  • Le Grand Monarque — Azay-le-RideauConsidered as a replacement and rejected: no lunch or dinner service.
  • Le Choiseul — AmboiseConsidered as a replacement and rejected: Michelin-starred, which fails the deliberate no-star criterion.
Compiled 8 August 2026 from each hotel's own photography, the Michelin Guide and the Sarthe and Vallée du Loir tourist boards. Room rates and menu prices are as published and move with the season — confirm on booking. Full notes in vault/Holidays/France September 2026.md.
